warmup.q: A service's GC log shows young pauses ending at a flat 300 MB for days, yet the pod's memory keeps growing until it is OOM-killed. Where should you look first?
options: A heap dump: the leak must be in the heap
Native memory: direct buffers, threads, metaspace, with Native Memory Tracking
warmup.why: A flat floor after young pauses means the live heap isn't growing, so a heap dump will look normal. The growth is outside the heap, where only NMT, the direct buffer pool and the thread count can show it. The young generation size and the pause goal change how the heap is collected, not what grows beside it.

sections.h: A Java leak is memory that stays reachable
sections.html:
In C, a leak is memory nobody can reach any more. In Java it's the opposite: the garbage collector frees everything unreachable, so a Java leak is memory that stays reachable from a GC root after the program is done with it. The GC is doing its job. Your code still holds the reference.

Here's the classic one in payment services, an idempotency cache with no eviction:

Java
static final Map<String, CachedResponse> IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

static CachedResponse handle(String requestId) {
    return IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE.computeIfAbsent(requestId, id -> new CachedResponse(id, 1_999, new byte[2_048]));
}
Kotlin
val IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CachedResponse>()

fun handle(requestId: String): CachedResponse =
    IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE.computeIfAbsent(requestId) { id -> CachedResponse(id, 1_999, ByteArray(2_048)) }

Every request adds an entry, and nothing ever removes one. Lesson 6 showed the symptom in a GC log: the after-values of young pauses rise pass after pass, full GCs free less and less, and in the end the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError or spends its time in Pause Full.

The same shape shows up in four places, over and over:

  • maps and caches without a bound or an expiry;
  • ThreadLocal values on pooled threads that nobody removes (the threads track showed a pool thread keeping one forever);
  • listeners and callbacks registered and never unregistered (lesson 3's weak registry is one fix);
  • class loaders that can't be unloaded, which shows up as metaspace growth and GC causes like Metadata GC Threshold, mostly in dev mode and test suites that reload code.

The first tool is a class histogram: a count of live objects per class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram prints it after a full GC, so it counts only reachable objects. For the cache above, after 20,000 requests:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
   1:         52255       43124072  [B (java.base@21.0.12.1)
   2:         32139         771336  java.lang.String (java.base@21.0.12.1)
   3:         22615         723680  java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap$Node (java.base@21.0.12.1)
   4:         20000         640000  workbench.memory.l07.LeakDemo$CachedResponse

[B means byte[]. The histogram tells you what fills the heap. It can't tell you who holds it. 20,000 of something you didn't expect to keep is the clue to follow next.

sections.h: A heap dump and its dominator tree show who holds it
sections.html:
A heap dump is a file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, in the HPROF format. You can get one three ways:

  • jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof from a running JVM. Its help text says "Impact: High": it does a full GC first (unless you pass -all) and pauses the JVM while it writes. -gz compresses the file, and JDK 24 and later add -parallel for more writer threads.
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with -XX:HeapDumpPath=..., so the JVM writes one at the moment it runs out. It's off by default. It's also a manageable flag, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true turns it on in a running JVM.
  • HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap(path, true) from code, which is what the demo uses.

Open the dump in Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer). Two sizes matter. The shallow size of an object is its own bytes, lesson 1's header-plus-fields. Its retained size is everything that would be freed if that one object were gone: the object plus everything reachable only through it.

You can compute retained size by hand on a small graph, and doing it once makes MAT's numbers obvious. Look at the figure. The static field holds the map, the map holds a table, the table holds 20,000 nodes, each node holds a key and a response, and each response holds a 2 KB receipt. Every path from a root to a receipt goes through the map, so the map dominates the receipts, and they are in its retained set. Add it up: 20,000 receipts at 2,064 bytes, 20,000 keys at 80, 20,000 responses at 32, 20,000 nodes at 32 and the table: about 44 MB. The shared "EUR" string is different. A currency catalog reaches it too, so removing the map wouldn't free it, and it isn't in the map's retained set.

MAT's dominator tree lists objects by retained size, biggest first. For a leak like this one, the map should sit at the top with about 44 MB, and its path to a GC root names the static field that holds it. (I couldn't run MAT for this course, so that's what the dominator tree's definition predicts for this dump, not a screenshot.) The histogram said "byte arrays". The dominator tree says "this map, held by this field".

sections.h: Native Memory Tracking finds growth outside the heap
sections.html:
Sometimes the heap is fine and the process still grows. The GC log shows a flat floor, a heap dump shows nothing odd, and the pod still gets OOM-killed (lesson 6). The memory is outside the heap, where heap dumps can't see.

Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's account of its own native memory. It's off by default. Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then ask a running process:

jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB

In the demo, a JVM with a 256 MB heap committed 294 MB at startup. After it allocated one 64 MiB direct buffer and started 100 threads, it had committed 369 MB. NMT shows where the difference went: Other went from nothing to 64 MB (the direct buffer), and Thread went from 1 MB to 11 MB committed, with 121 MB reserved, because each new thread reserves about 1 MB of stack but touches only a little of it.

For a slow leak, take a baseline and compare later:

jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB

The diff marks every change: in one test, Other (reserved=100MB +100MB, committed=100MB +100MB) after 100 direct buffers of 1 MiB. A growing Other points at direct buffers or native code; a growing Thread at threads you start and never stop; a growing Class or Metaspace at class loaders.

Direct buffers deserve one more level of detail. A ByteBuffer.allocateDirect call creates a small object on the heap that owns the native memory, and a phantom-reference cleaner, the same idea as lesson 3's Cleaner, frees that memory after the GC collects the small object. So native memory waits for a garbage collection, and a big, quiet heap may not collect for a long time. Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the limit for all of it is the max heap size. Set it, and a leak fails loudly instead of quietly: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 67108864 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 33554432), with a stack trace that points at the code.

try.title: Watch native memory move
steps: Read NmtDemo. Its first child runs with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and prints NMT's summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 threads. Its second child allocates 64 MiB of direct memory under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m.
Predict which NMT categories change, and by how much. Then run it.

code.title: NmtDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l07; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import javax.management.ObjectName; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Native Memory Tracking from inside a child JVM: the summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer * and 100 extra threads. Then a direct buffer that doesn't fit under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize. */ public class NmtDemo { static final Pattern CATEGORY = Pattern.compile("^-?\\s*(Total|[A-Z][\\w ]+?):? \\(?reserved=(\\d+)MB, committed=(\\d+)MB"); static String nativeMemory() throws Exception { // the same as: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB return (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); } static void print(String title) throws Exception { System.out.println(title); for (String line : nativeMemory().lines().toList()) { Matcher m = CATEGORY.matcher(line); if (m.find()) System.out.printf(" %-20s committed %,5d MB (reserved %,5d MB)%n", m.group(1), Long.parseLong(m.group(3)), Long.parseLong(m.group(2))); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "track"); Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "limit"); return; } if (args[0].equals("limit")) { try { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) { System.out.println("with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m: " + e); } return; } print("at startup"); ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); // what Netty does for socket buffers CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { never.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } }); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } print("after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 more threads"); System.out.println("buffer " + direct.capacity()); } }

sections.h: Arenas give off-heap memory a lifetime you control
sections.html:
The Foreign Function and Memory API (FFM), final since JDK 22 (JEP 454), gives off-heap memory a lifetime you control. Memory comes from an arena, and the arena decides when it's freed:

Arena Lifetime Closed by Threads
Arena.global() until the JVM exits nobody any
Arena.ofAuto() until the GC finds it unreachable the GC any
Arena.ofConfined() until you call close() you, from the owner thread the owner only
Arena.ofShared() until you call close() you, from any thread any

A confined arena in try-with-resources frees its memory at the closing brace. No GC is involved, so there's nothing to wait for. And if code uses a segment after its arena is closed, it gets an IllegalStateException ("Already closed"), not a crash or silently corrupted memory as with freed memory in C.

Java
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024);   // 32 MiB off-heap
    ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999);
}                                                               // freed here
Kotlin
Arena.ofConfined().use { arena ->
    val ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024)              // 32 MiB off-heap
    ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999)
}                                                               // freed here

Native segments count against the same limit as direct buffers. Per the JDK 25 source, allocating one reserves memory through the same accounting as ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, and on JDK 21's preview of the API, a 32 MiB segment under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m failed with Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory.

The labs compile for JDK 21, where FFM is still a preview, so this lesson's FFM demo is a single file that runs outside Gradle on JDK 22 or later.

try.title: Free 32 MiB at a closing brace (JDK 22 or later)
steps: This one runs outside Gradle and needs JDK 22 or later, ideally 25. Check with java -version. From labs/, run java memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc: the commands are at the top of ArenaDemo.kt.
Predict the three numbers it prints, then run it.
Run it again with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m placed right after java.

code.title: ArenaDemo.java (JDK 22 or later)
code.html: // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. From labs/: // java memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java import java.lang.foreign.Arena; import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment; import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; public class ArenaDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { long before = directBytes(); // the JDK may already hold a little MemorySegment escaped; try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 1. one owner thread, closed by try-with-resources MemorySegment ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (long i = 0; i < ledger.byteSize() / Long.BYTES; i++) { ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100); // 4 million longs, and no objects } System.out.println("entry 1,000 holds " + ledger.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)); System.out.printf("inside the arena: %+d MiB of direct memory%n", (directBytes() - before) >> 20); escaped = ledger; } // 3. freed here, not by the GC System.out.printf("after close(): %+d MiB of direct memory%n", (directBytes() - before) >> 20); try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0); // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("reading after close() throws: " + e.getMessage()); } } // native segments are counted, and limited, together with direct ByteBuffers static long directBytes() { return ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class).stream() .filter(p -> p.getName().equals("direct")) .mapToLong(BufferPoolMXBean::getMemoryUsed).sum(); } }

alt.title: ArenaDemo.kt (JDK 22 or later)
alt.html: // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. import java.lang.foreign.Arena import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // native segments are counted, and limited, together with direct ByteBuffers fun directBytes(): Long = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" } .sumOf { it.memoryUsed } fun main(args: Array<String>) { // args unused; one main keeps every launcher happy val before = directBytes() // the JDK may already hold a little val escaped: MemorySegment Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 1. one owner thread, closed by use {} val ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (i in 0 until ledger.byteSize() / Long.SIZE_BYTES) { ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100) // 4 million longs, and no objects } println("entry 1,000 holds ${ledger.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)}") println("inside the arena: %+d MiB of direct memory".format((directBytes() - before) shr 20)) escaped = ledger } // 3. freed here, not by the GC println("after close(): %+d MiB of direct memory".format((directBytes() - before) shr 20)) try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0) // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("reading after close() throws: ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: entry 1,000 holds 100000, then +32 MiB of direct memory inside the arena and +0 MiB after close(), and reading after close() throws: Already closed. With the 16 MB limit, arena.allocate fails with OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory. These outputs come from JDK 21's preview of the same API; the methods used here are the same in the final API of JDK 22 and later.

refs.title: Arena source at jdk-25-ga: the four kinds of arena

analogy: A dominator tree answers one question for every object: if I cut this one rope, how much falls? The heap is a set of loads hanging from hooks in the ceiling, the GC roots, by ropes that are references. Some loads hang from one rope; others are tied to two hooks. Cut the rope above the cache and 44 MB of receipts fall, because every rope to them ran through it. Cut a rope above something that also hangs from another hook, and nothing falls. Retained size is the weight that falls. Where it breaks: real ropes are cut once. In a heap, your code ties new ropes on every request, so you find the rope in a dump, but you fix it in the code that keeps tying it.
world: In a payment platform the usual suspects are easy to list. Idempotency caches and duplicate-detection maps that never evict. Per-merchant maps keyed by something that is created per request. A ThreadLocal buffer on Kafka consumer or worker threads that nobody removes. A Temporal or Kafka listener registered for each new tenant and never removed. And outside the heap: a Netty-based client that allocates direct buffers per call without releasing them, or a native HSM or compression library. Decide which half to look at from the GC log first. A rising floor means a heap dump and the dominator tree. A flat floor with a growing pod means NMT with a baseline and a diff.
mistake: Taking a heap dump to explain an OOM-killed pod. The kernel killed the process because the whole process outgrew its limit, and the heap was often fine: a heap dump shows only the heap, so it looks healthy and the team concludes the problem is random. People make the mistake because the heap is the only memory most tools show. The fix is to read the evidence in order: if the GC log's floor is flat, turn on -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, take a baseline, and diff it after the growth; cap -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize so a direct-buffer leak becomes an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill.

compare.title: A bounded LRU cache in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LruCache.java
java.html: final class LruCache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> map; LruCache(int maxEntries) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }; } synchronized V get(K key) { return map.get(key); } synchronized void put(K key, V value) { map.put(key, value); } }

kotlin.title: LruCache.kt
kotlin.html: class LruCache<K, V>(private val maxEntries: Int) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?): Boolean = size > maxEntries } @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? = map[key] @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) { map[key] = value } }

compare.note: Both build on the same JDK class, and both need the lock: LinkedHashMap isn't thread-safe, and in access order even get changes the map. Java overrides removeEldestEntry in an anonymous subclass; Kotlin does it with an object : expression, and its eldest parameter is nullable because the JDK doesn't annotate it. Kotlin returns V? from get, which makes the cache miss visible in the type. In a real service you'd often reach for a cache library with size limits and expiry, but the leak fix is the same idea in every form: decide a maximum and make the structure enforce it.

worked.title: From OOMKilled to the line that leaks

steps.say: An invented settlement API restarts with exit code 137 every two days. Start with the GC log, because it decides which half of memory to look at. Here the young pauses end at about 300 MB, day after day: the live heap is flat. A heap dump would look healthy, so don't start there.
steps.code:
GC(9120) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1490M->301M(1536M) 9.420ms
GC(9121) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1488M->298M(1536M) 9.112ms

steps.say: 1. Measure native memory. Restart one instance with NMT, take a baseline once it's warm, and diff a few hours later. Only one category moved.
steps.code:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary ... -jar settlement-api.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# four hours later
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB
-                     Other (reserved=812MB +544MB, committed=812MB +544MB)
                            (malloc=812MB +544MB #9310 +6480)

steps.say: 1. Name the suspect. Other growing by thousands of mallocs is direct buffers or native code. The JDK's direct buffer pool confirms it: its count and size keep climbing. Find who allocates direct buffers per request. Here it's a report generator that keeps one per merchant report in a map and never removes them.
steps.code: // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per report, kept forever private final Map<String, ByteBuffer> reportBuffers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); ByteBuffer bufferFor(String reportId) { return reportBuffers.computeIfAbsent(reportId, id -> ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20)); }

alt.html: // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per report, kept forever private val reportBuffers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ByteBuffer>() fun bufferFor(reportId: String): ByteBuffer = reportBuffers.computeIfAbsent(reportId) { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 shl 20) }

steps.say: 1. Fix the lifetime, then add a guard. Give each report its memory for exactly as long as it's being written, with a confined arena (JDK 22 or later), or remove the buffer from the map when the report is done. Then cap direct memory, so the next leak of this kind fails as an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill.
steps.code: void writeReport(String reportId, Report report) { try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the report MemorySegment buffer = arena.allocate(1 << 20); report.renderInto(buffer); upload(reportId, buffer); } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

alt.html: fun writeReport(reportId: String, report: Report) { Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the report val buffer = arena.allocate(1 shl 20) report.renderInto(buffer) upload(reportId, buffer) } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

lab.title: Find and fix the leaks in an idempotency cache
steps: Run the tests. Four of six fail. The two that pass check behaviour: a retry gets the same response, and a reused key with a different body is rejected. Keep those passing.

Read the failing messages. Two tests count live objects with the class histogram, the same one jcmd GC.class_histogram prints: 20,000 responses and 20,000 requests are still alive after 20,000 payments.
Fix the first leak: bound the cache to maxEntries with an access-ordered LinkedHashMap and removeEldestEntry, and make the methods synchronized.

Run again. The request test still fails, now with about 500. Find out why each entry keeps its whole PaymentRequest, and replace it with what the retry check really needs: a SHA-256 digest of the body.
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) makes the map access-ordered. Override removeEldestEntry to return size() > maxEntries.
MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(body) gives 32 bytes. Compare two digests with MessageDigest.isEqual.
The entry record is private: you can change its fields freely, for example to record Entry(byte[] bodyDigest, PaymentResponse response).
The leak tests allow 2 stray objects, because the test's own last local variables may still be reachable while it counts.

drill.title: Write the first-response commands from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. A pod is growing. Write the commands you'd run, in order, to decide whether it's a heap leak or native growth, and to collect evidence for each case. Then write a bounded LRU map from memory.

answer.html: // 1. which half? read the floor of the young pauses in the GC log (rising = heap, flat = native) // 2. heap: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram (what) // jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof (who: dominator tree in MAT) // 3. native: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB static <K, V> Map<K, V> lru(int maxEntries) { return Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }); }

alt.html: // 1. which half? read the floor of the young pauses in the GC log (rising = heap, flat = native) // 2. heap: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram (what) // jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof (who: dominator tree in MAT) // 3. native: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB fun <K, V> lru(maxEntries: Int): MutableMap<K, V> = Collections.synchronizedMap(object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?) = size > maxEntries })

recap: A Java leak is memory that stays reachable from a GC root after you're done with it: unbounded caches, ThreadLocals on pooled threads, forgotten listeners, class loaders.
A rising floor in the GC log means a heap leak. jcmd GC.class_histogram says what fills the heap; a heap dump says who holds it.
Retained size is what would be freed if one object went away. The dominator tree in MAT ranks objects by it and leads you to the field that holds the leak.
A flat floor with a growing pod means native memory. Start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, take a baseline, and read summary.diff.
Direct buffers are freed only after a GC collects their small heap objects, and their default limit is the max heap. Set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize so a leak fails loudly.
FFM arenas (final in JDK 22) free off-heap memory at close(). Native segments count against the same limit as direct buffers.

explain.prompt: Explain to an on-call colleague, in your own words, how you'd go from "the pod keeps growing" to the line of code that leaks, for both kinds of leak.
explain.answer: First I'd read the GC log, because it says which half of memory is growing. If the after-values of young pauses keep rising, it's the heap: a class histogram shows which classes pile up, and a heap dump opened in MAT shows who holds them. The dominator tree ranks objects by retained size, what would be freed if they went away, and the path to a GC root names the static field, the thread or the map. If the floor is flat but the pod grows, it's native memory: I'd restart one instance with Native Memory Tracking, take a baseline, and diff it later to see which category grows. Other points at direct buffers or native code, Thread at threads that never end, Class or Metaspace at class loaders. Then I'd fix the lifetime in code, bound caches, and set MaxDirectMemorySize so the next leak fails with a stack trace.

deeper.html:
A few details make leak hunting faster.

A histogram is cheap enough to take twice. Take one, wait ten minutes under load, take another, and compare instance counts: the class whose count only goes up is your lead, even before you have a dump. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all skips the full GC and counts unreachable objects too, which is useful when you can't afford the pause and dangerous when you forget the flag.

Heap dumps are large: about the size of the live heap, here 50 MB for 44 MB of leak. GC.heap_dump -gz=1 compresses while writing. Writing a dump pauses the JVM, so in a cluster take it from one instance after you've taken it out of the load balancer.

MAT's GC roots have kinds, and the kind is a clue. A System Class root means a static field. A Thread root, "a started, but not stopped, thread" in MAT's words, means something reachable from a live thread: its stack or its thread-locals. JNI Global means native code is holding a reference.

Class loader leaks look different from object leaks. Each redeploy or hot reload creates a new class loader with new classes. If anything from outside still references one object of an old class, for example a JDBC driver registered in a global list, a ThreadLocal on a shared thread or a static cache in a library, the whole old class loader and every class it loaded stay in metaspace. NMT shows Class and Metaspace growing, and GC logs show collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold. In production Quarkus rarely reloads, but dev mode and long test suites do.

Finally, jol-cli can estimate how a heap dump's objects would lay out under other JVM settings. For the 50 MB dump from this lesson's research, it estimated 1.3% less with compact object headers and 3.2% more without compressed references: a dump full of 2 KB arrays gains little from smaller headers, as lesson 1 predicted.
